read.sections.0.heading.source: It learns patterns from huge amounts of text
read.sections.0.heading.back: An LLM learns patterns from very large amounts of text

read.sections.0.text.source: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing. Many chatbots today are built on a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from a huge amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages. Much of it was written by people. From it, the model learns patterns, for example which words often come after other words. It works with small pieces of text, called tokens. A token may be a word or part of a word. Look at the made-up word game at Lakeside Learning Centre. After “a cup of”, its practice sentences had “tea” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once.
read.sections.0.text.back: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with through writing. Many chatbots now are built on a large language model, or LLM (from the English large language model). An LLM learns from very large amounts of text, such as books, articles and web pages. Most of that text was written by people. From that text, the model learns patterns, for example which words often come after other words. This model works with small pieces of text, called tokens. A token can be one word or part of a word. Look at the made-up word game at Lakeside Learning Centre. After “a cup of”, its practice sentences had “tea” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Much of it was written by people" became "sebagian besar teks itu" (most of that text). The teachers' note explains that not all of it is; "banyak dari teks itu" (much of that text) is closer if reviewers prefer. The letters LLM come from English, so the English name is given once.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: A chatbot is a program you can chat with. Many chatbots use a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from lots of text, like books and web pages. People wrote much of it. The LLM finds patterns in the words. It works with tokens. A token is a word or part of a word. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came most often after “a cup of”.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A chatbot is a program you can chat with. Many chatbots use a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from lots of text, like books and web pages. Much of that text was written by people. The LLM finds patterns in the words. The LLM works with tokens. A token is one word or part of a word. In the word game at Lakeside, “tea” appeared most often after “a cup of”.

read.sections.1.heading.source: It writes one piece at a time
read.sections.1.heading.back: An LLM writes one piece each time

read.sections.1.text.source: When you ask an LLM a question, it predicts the next token of its answer, adds it, and predicts the one after it, again and again. Often each token is picked partly by chance from the likely ones, so the Lakeside model would often say “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time. Chatbots are not new: in 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules that people wrote. LLMs use machine learning instead. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks. ChatGPT, released on 30 November 2022, made LLMs famous.
read.sections.1.text.back: When you ask an LLM a question, the LLM predicts the next token of its answer, adds it, then predicts the token after it, again and again. Often each token is picked partly at random from the likely tokens, so the Lakeside model would often say “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time. Chatbots are not new: in 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules that people wrote. LLMs use machine learning. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks. ChatGPT, released on 30 November 2022, made LLMs famous.
read.sections.1.text.note: "LLMs use machine learning instead": "instead" is carried by the contrast with the sentence before rather than a separate word.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: You ask an LLM a question. It predicts the next token, again and again. Often it picks partly by chance. So the Lakeside model often says “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, it gives the same answer each time. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, one followed rules that people wrote. LLMs learn from examples instead. Researchers made a new design in 2017. In November 2022, ChatGPT made them famous.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: You ask an LLM a question. The LLM predicts the next token, again and again. Often the LLM picks partly at random. So the Lakeside model often says “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, a model gives the same answer every time. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, there was a chatbot that followed rules that people wrote. LLMs learn from examples. Researchers made a new design in 2017. In November 2022, ChatGPT made LLMs famous.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Sounding sure is not the same as being right
read.sections.2.heading.back: Sounding sure is not the same as right

read.sections.2.text.source: A basic LLM predicts words that sound right. It does not check facts the way a careful person does. So it can make things up, and it can sound very confident even when it is wrong. At Lakeside, the pretend helper named a book that does not exist. Some tools also search the web and show links, but the pages can be wrong or misread, so you still need to check them. Most big LLMs learned mainly from English text, and researchers have found they work worse in languages with little writing online. So check important answers with a trusted source, such as a library or a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.back: A basic LLM predicts words that sound right. An LLM does not check facts the way a careful person does. So an LLM can make things up, and can sound very sure even when it is wrong. At Lakeside, the pretend helper tool named a book that does not exist. Some tools also search the internet and show links, but those pages can be wrong or misread, so you still need to check them. Most big LLMs learned mainly from English text, and researchers found that LLMs work worse in languages that have only a little writing on the internet. So check important answers with a trusted source, such as a library or a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Confident" (the key word) as "yakin" (sure). "Percaya diri" is the usual word for a confident person but sounds odd for an answer.

write.example.source: A large language model learns from a huge amount of text, much of it written by people. It writes an answer by predicting the next token, a word or part of a word, again and again. It can be useful for explaining ideas or translating short notices. But it can be wrong because it picks words that sound right. It does not check facts. At Lakeside, the helper named a book that does not exist, and it sounded sure. Before I trust an answer, I check a trusted source, like a library or a teacher.
write.example.back: A large language model learns from very large amounts of text, much of which was written by people. The model writes an answer by predicting the next token, one word or part of a word, again and again. The model can be useful for explaining ideas or translating short announcements. But the model can be wrong because it picks words that sound right. The model does not check facts. At Lakeside, the helper tool named a book that does not exist, and its answer sounded sure. Before I trust an answer, I check a trusted source, like a library or a teacher.

watch.summary.source: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a huge amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, worked out very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts which letter often comes after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer pieces, like whole words, its guesses get much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped to make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.
watch.summary.back: In this video, two people who make AI tools explain how chatbots work. One of them works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from very large amounts of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. The model uses numbers about what is likely to come, calculated very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. The program counts which letter often comes after each letter. When the program writes this way, the words look strange. When the program looks at longer pieces, like whole words, its guesses become much better. Big models use artificial neural networks, which loosely copy the brain. People also helped make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so the model can make mistakes.
watch.summary.note: "Neural networks" as "jaringan saraf tiruan" (artificial neural networks), the standard Indonesian term.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Never ask learners whether they use chatbots, which ones, or what they have typed into one. Some have never used one; others may have shared private things. Use the Lakeside examples.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Never ask learners whether they use chatbots, which chatbots, or what they have typed there. Some have never used one; others may have shared private things. Use the examples from Lakeside.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Don't ask which languages learners speak at home, or which language a tool got wrong for them. Let them say so if they want to.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Don't ask which languages learners use at home, or which language a tool handled wrongly for them. Let them say it themselves if they want to.

educatorNotes.0.source: There is no real chatbot in the app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are made up. The cup-of-tea game is a toy analogy, not a full account: real LLMs work on tokens and far more text, and the lesson's “word” is a simplification. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so the lesson says “much of it”. A model can repeat an answer: an app can pick the likeliest token every time, or pick at random among likely ones (Google's course).
educatorNotes.0.back: There is no real chatbot in this app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper tool's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are all made up. The cup-of-tea game is a simple comparison, not a full explanation: real LLMs work with tokens and much more text, and the lesson's “word” is a simplification. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so the lesson says “most” or “much”. A model can repeat the same answer: an app can pick the most likely token every time, or pick at random among the likely tokens (Google's course).
educatorNotes.0.note: The English note quotes the lesson's "much of it"; the Indonesian reading says "sebagian besar" (standard) and "banyak" (simpler), so the note names both.

educatorNotes.1.source: A basic model writes from what it learned; some tools also search the web and show links. A link is not proof: open it and check it, as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT's lesson on fact-checking AI search results). The 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani and others). Paper version of the activity: write the nine sentences on cards and sort them into “Can”, “Can't” and “Hard to say”; reward reasons.
educatorNotes.1.back: A basic model writes from what it has learned; some tools also search the internet and show links. A link is not proof: open it and check it, as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT's lesson on checking facts in AI search results). The 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani and others). Paper version of this activity: write the nine sentences on cards, then sort them into “Can”, “Can't” and “Hard to be sure”; value the reasons.
